1.problem: Let \(x_i, y_i\) \((i=1,2,\cdots,n)\) be real numbers such that \[x_1\ge x_2\ge\cdots\ge x_n \text{ and } y_1\ge y_2\ge\cdots\ge y_n.\] Prove that, if \(z_1, z_2,\cdots, z_n\) is any permutation of \(y_1, y_2, \cdots, y_n,\) then \[\sum^n_{i=1}(x_i-y_i)^2\le\sum^n_{i=1}(x_i-z_i)^2.\]
1.solutions:
Video Solution (In Chinese)

https://youtu.be/3-iF4zIxsUQ

Solution

We can expand and simplify the inequality a bit, and using the fact that \(z\) is a permutation of \(y\), we can cancel some terms.

\[\sum^n_{i=1}x_i^2 + \sum^n_{i=1}y_i^2 - 2\sum^n_{i=1}x_iy_i \leq \sum^n_{i=1}x_i^2 + \sum^n_{i=1}z_i^2 - 2\sum^n_{i=1}x_iz_i\]

\[\sum^n_{i=1}x_iy_i \geq \sum^n_{i=1}x_iz_i\]

Consider the pairing \(x_1 ightarrow y_1\), \(x_2 ightarrow y_2\), ... \(x_n ightarrow y_n\). By switching around some of the \(y\) values, we have obtained the pairing \(x_1 ightarrow z_1\), \(x_2 ightarrow z_2\), ... \(x_n ightarrow z_n\). Suppose that we switch around two \(y\)-values, \(y_m\) and \(y_n\), such that \(y_m > y_n\). If \(x_m > x_n\), call this a type 1 move. Otherwise, call this a type 2 move.

Type 2 moves only increase the sum of the products of the pairs. The sum is increased by \(x_n \cdot y_m + x_m \cdot y_n - x_m \cdot y_m - x_n \cdot y_n\). This is equivalent to \((x_n - x_m)(y_m - y_n)\), which is clearly nonnegative since \(y_m > y_n\) and \(x_n > x_m\).

We will now consider switching from the \(x\)-\(z\) pairing back to the \(x\)-\(y\) pairing. We will prove that from any pairing of \(x\) and \(z\) values, you can use just type 2 moves to navigate back to the pairing of \(x\) and \(y\) values, which will complete the proof.

Suppose that \(x_a\) is the biggest \(x\)-value that is not paired with its \(y\)-value in the \(x\) and \(z\) pairing. Then, switch this \(y\)-value with the \(y\)-value currently paired with \(x_a\). This is obviously a type 2 move. Continue this process until you reach back to the \(x\)-\(y\) pairing. All moves are type 2 moves, so the proof is complete.

~mathboy100

Solution 2

We can rewrite the summation as

\[\sum^n_{i=1} x_i^2 + \sum^n_{i=1} y_i^2 - \sum^n_{i=1}x_iy_i \le \sum^n_{i=1} x_i^2 + \sum^n_{i=1} z_i^2 - \sum^n_{i=1}x_iz_i.\]

Since \(\sum^n_{i=1} y_i^2 = \sum^n_{i=1} z_i^2\), the above inequality is equivalent to

\[\sum^n_{i=1}x_iy_i \ge \sum^n_{i=1}x_iz_i.\]

We will now prove that the left-hand side of the inequality is the greatest sum reached out of all possible values of \(\sum^n_{i=1}x_iz_i\). Obviously, if \(x_1 = x_2 = \ldots = x_n\) or \(y_1 = y_2 = \ldots = y_n\), the inequality is true. Now, assume, for contradiction, that neither of those conditions are true and that there exists some order of \(z_i\)s that are not ordered in the form \(z_1 \ge z_2 \ge \ldots \ge z_n\) such that \(\sum^n_{i=1}x_iz_i\) is at a maximum out of all possible permutations and is greater than the sum \(\sum^n_{i=1}x_iy_i\). This necessarily means that in the sum \(\sum^n_{i=1}x_iz_i\) there exists two terms \(x_pz_m\) and \(x_qz_n\) such that \(x_p > x_q\) and \(z_m < z_n\). Notice that

\[x_pz_n + x_qz_m - (x_pz_m + x_qz_n) = (x_p-x_q)(z_n-z_m) > 0,\]

which means if we make the terms \(x_pz_n\) and \(x_qz_m\) instead of the original \(x_pz_m\) and \(x_qz_n\), we can achieve a higher sum. However, this is impossible, since we assumed we had the highest sum. Thus, the inequality

\[\sum^n_{i=1}x_iy_i \ge \sum^n_{i=1}x_iz_i\]

is proved, which is equivalent to what we wanted to prove.

~Imajinary

Remark

It is only the most common way of rearrangement inequality after expanding and subtracting same terms.~bluesoul

Remarks (added by pf02, November 2025)

\(\mathbf{1}\) The first solution can not be called a solution. There are several issues with it. The first issue is that the notion of "pairing" is not defined. The notions "type 1 move" vs. "type 2 move" are defined only very loosely. The way they are used contradicts the fact that they are meant to be complementary. Indeed, we can not assume we have only strict inequalities among the \(x\)’s and the \(y\)’s.

The second issue is with the last paragraph. Consider the sentences "Suppose that \(x_a\) is the biggest \(x\)-value that is not paired with its \(y\)-value in the \(x\) and \(z\) pairing. Then, switch this \(y\)-value with the \(y\)-value currently paired with \(x_a\)." These two sentences do not make sense. Furthermore, depending on what meaning we would want to force on these two sentences, and on what "type 2 move" may mean, the sentence which follows, "This is obviously a type 2 move" may or may not be true. And finally, the sentence "Continue this process until you reach back to the \(x\)-\(y\) pairing" is unclear: it is not clear that we would reach "the \(x\)-\(y\) pairing" (whatever "pairing" may mean).

\(\mathbf{2}\) Solution 2 is incorrect. The author assumed that \(x_pz_m\) and \(x_qz_n\) are terms in \(\sum^n_{i=1}x_iz_i\), but this is not true unless \(p = m\) and \(q = n\).

(Never mind the fact that there is a crucial sentence which does not make sense: "assume, for contradiction, that neither of those conditions are true and that there exists some order of \(z_i\)s that are not ordered in the form \(z_1 \ge z_2 \ge \ldots \ge z_n\) such that \(\sum^n_{i=1}x_iz_i\) is at a maximum out of all possible permutations and is greater than the sum \(\sum^n_{i=1}x_iy_i\)". But a benign and eager reader can guess what the author most likely wanted to express in this sentence.)

\(\mathbf{3}\) The remark which follows the two "solutions" makes no sense at all.

\(\mathbf{4}\) Below I will give a solution to the problem.

Solution 3

Let \(S = \{y_1, y_2, \cdots, y_n\}\) be the given set of numbers, \(y_1 \ge y_2 \ge \cdots \ge y_n\), and let \(\{z_1, z_2, \cdots, z_n\}\) be a permutation of the set \(S\). In other words \(z_j = \sigma(y_i)\) for a one-to-one function \(\sigma: S ightarrow S\). Remember that a transposition is a permutation such that there exist \(i, j\) such that \(\sigma(y_i) = y_j, \sigma(y_j) = y_i\) and \(\sigma(y_k) = y_k\) for all \(k e i, j\). In other words, a transposition swaps two elements of \(S\), and leaves the others in place. Remember that we can combine permutations. Explicitely, if \(\sigma_1, \sigma_2\) are two permutations, \(\sigma_1 : \{y_i\} ightarrow \{z_j\} = \{\sigma_1(y_i)\}\) and \(\sigma_2 : \{z_j\} ightarrow \{z_{k}^{(2)}\} = \{\sigma_2(z_j)\}\) then we have the combined permutation \(\sigma = \sigma_2 \circ \sigma_1\) which is \(\sigma : \{y_i\} ightarrow \{z_{k}^{(2)}\} = \{\sigma_2(\sigma_1((y_i))\}.\)

For the purposes of the solution to this problem, we will think of the elements of the set \(S\) as arranged in a sequence, specifically, the sequence created by the last permutation applied. For example if we swap \(10\) and \(22\) in the set (or sequence) \(\{27, 22, 14, 10, 8, 5\}\), the new set (or sequence) will be \(\{27, 10, 14, 22, 8, 5\}\). This way, each element in the permuted set has a precisely defined index.

We will call a transposition \(\mathbf{adjacent}\) if it swaps two nearby (or neighboring) elements of \(S\). In other words \(\sigma\) is adjacent, if it permutes \(\{z_1, \dots, z_i, z_{i+1}, \dots, z_n\}\) into \(\{z_1, \dots, z_{i+1}, z_i, \dots, z_n\}\). We will call a transposition \(\mathbf{positive}\) if given \(i < j\) and the elements \(z_i, z_j\) being swapped, the inequality \(z_i \ge z_j\) is satisfied.

The statement of the problem will follow from the following two lemmas:

\(\mathbf{Lemma\ 1}\) If \(\sigma\) is a positive transposition \(\sigma : \{z_j\} ightarrow \{z_{k}^{(2)}\} = \{\sigma(z_j)\}\) then \(\sum^n_{i=1}(x_i - z_i)^2 \le \sum^n_{i=1}(x_i - z_i^{(2)})^2.\)

\(\mathbf{Lemma\ 2}\) Every permutation \(\sigma\) of the set \(S = \{y_i\}_{i=1,\dots,n}\) with \(y_1 \ge y_2 \ge \dots \ge y_n\) is the combination of adjacent, positive transpositions.

Let us prove the problem assuming the lemmas. According to Lemma 2, we can write a given permutation as \(\sigma = \sigma_m \circ \sigma_{m-1} \circ \dots \circ \sigma_1\), where each \(\sigma_k\) is an adjacent, positive permutation. If \(\{z_i\}\) is the resulting sequence from \(\sigma\) and \(\{z_i^{(k)}\}\) are the resulting sequences from \(\sigma_k\) then \(z_i = z_i^{(m)}\) for each \(i\). According to Lemma 1, using that each \(\sigma_k\) is positive, we have

\(\sum^n_{i=1}(x_i - y_i)^2 \le \sum^n_{i=1}(x_i - z_i^{(1)})^2 \le \sum^n_{i=1}(x_i - z_i^{(2)})^2 \le \dots \le \sum^n_{i=1}(x_i - z_i^{(m)})^2 = \sum^n_{i=1}(x_i - z_i)^2.\)

We will now prove the two lemmas.

\(\mathbf{Proof\ of\ lemma\ 1}\) This is a very easy computation. Let \(z_p, z_q\) be transposed, \(p < q\) and \(z_p \ge z_q\). Since \(z_i\) does not change for \(i e p, q\) we just have to verify that \((x_p - z_p)^2 + (x_q - z_q)^2 \le (x_p - z_q)^2 + (x_q - z_p)^2\). This becomes \(x_p z_p + x_q z_q \ge x_p z_q + x_q z_p\), or \((x_p - x_q) (z_p - z_q) \ge 0\), which is true by assumption.

\(\mathbf{Proof\ of\ lemma\ 2}\) This is a little more complicated. We will prove it by induction. First, notice that the statement is true for \(n = 2\).

Assume the statement true for \(n-1\), and prove it for \(n\). Note that all permutations of \(S = \{y_i\}_{i=1, \dots, n}\) can be obtained by bringing \(y_k\) to position \(1\) (for \(k = 1, \dots, n\)), and shifting \(y_1, \dots, y_{k-1}\) to the right by one place, and then making all the possible permutations of the \(n-1\) elements \(\{y_1, \dots, y_{k-1}, y_{k+1}, \dots, y_n\}\) (which are now in positions \(2, \dots, n\)). (Just to verify, this way we are getting \(n imes (n-1)!\) permutations, which equals \(n!\) as expected (the number of permutations of \(S = \{y_i\}_{i=1,\dots,n}\).)

Let us verify that all this can be done using positive, adjacent transpositions. The case when we don’t move \(y_1\), but only permute \(\{y_i\}_{i=2, \dots, n}\) follows immediately from the induction assumption. For \(k > 1\), we make first a transposition of \(y_k, y_{k-1}\). In terms of positions in the sequence \(y_k\) has now \(y_{k-2}\) to the left, and \(y_{k-1}\) to the right. Make a transposition of \(y_k, y_{k-2}\). In terms of positions in the sequence \(y_k\) has now \(y_{k-3}\) to the left, and \(y_{k-2}\) to the right. Now make another transposition. Continue this process till \(y_k\) is at position \(1\), followed by \(\{y_1, \dots, y_{k-1}, y_{k+1}, \dots, y_n\}\). We can now apply the induction hypothesis to this sequence of \(n - 1\) non-increasing numbers.

This concludes the proof of lemma 2, and of the problem.

[Solution by pf02, November 2025]

Solution 4

I didn’t follow solution \(1\), but it sounded similar to my solution so I wasn’t going to add my solution. However, given the remarks that there may be problems with solution \(1\), I thought I’d add my version.

First we prove the result for \(n=2\). This is equivalent to showing \((x_1-y_1)^2 + (x_2-y_2)^2 \leq (x_1-y_2)^2 + (x_2-y_1)^2\) which is equivalent to (expanding and factorizing) \((x_1-x_2)(y_1-y_2) \geq 0\) which is clearly true. Let \(z_{j_1} = y_1\). We claim

\[(x_1-y_1)^2 + (x_{j_1} - z_1)^2 \leq (x_1-z_1)^2 + (x_{j_1}-z_{j_1})^2.\]

If \(z_1 = y_1\) (so that \(j_1 =1\)) we’re done. Otherwise \(z_1 eq y_1\). Clearly \(z_{j_1} = y_1 \geq z_1\). By the \(n=2\) case then, \((x_1-z_{j_1})^2 + (x_{j_1}-z_1)^2 \leq (x_1-z_1)^2 + (x_{j_1}-z_{j_1})^2\), which shows the claim. It follows

\[(x_1-y_1)^2 + (x_2-z_2)^2 + \cdots + (x_{j_1}-z_1)^2 + \cdots + (x_n - z_n)^2 \leq \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-z_i)^2. \ \ \ (1)\]

(Here the sum on the LHS is \(\sum_i (x_i-z_i)^2\) with the first term replaced by \((x_1-y_1)^2\) and the \(j_1^{ ext{th}}\) term replaced by \((x_{j_1}-z_1)^2\)). Let \(z_i' = z_i\) for \(i=2,...,j_1-1,j_1+1,...,n\) and \(z_{j_1}' = z_1\). Clearly, we can reapply the \(n-1\) version of \((1)\) to the LHS of \((1)\) to get (since \(x_2 \geq \cdots \geq x_n\) and \(y_2 \geq \cdots \geq y_n\) simply has a different permutation \(z_2',...,z_n'\))

\[(x_2-y_2)^2 + (x_3-z_3')^2 + \cdots + (x_{j_2}-z_2')^2 + \cdots + (x_n - z_n')^2 \leq \sum_{i=2}^n (x_i-z_i')^2 \ \ \ (2)\]

where \(j_2\) is such that \(z_{j_2}'=y_2\). Repeating this process for \((x_3-y_3)^2\), and then \((x_4-y_4)^2\), and so on, and chaining the inequalities (for example, adding \((x_1-y_1)^2\) to \((2)\) allows combining \((2)\) with \((1)\)), one will eventually be left with \(\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-y_i)^2 \leq \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i-z_i)^2\).

~not_detriti

Proof 5 (formal, inspired by Inequalities: A Mathematical Olympiad Approach)

The rearrangement inequality states

\[\sum_{i=1}^n x_iz_i \ge \sum_{i=1}^n x_iy_i\] .

The problem defines \(\sum y_i = \sum z_i\) so therefore one could subtract \(- 2 \sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i\) from both sides.

\[\sum_{i=1}^n x_{i}^2 - 2 \sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i + \sum_{i=1}^n y_i^2 \le \sum_{i=1}^n x_{i}^2 - 2 \sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i + \sum_{i=1}^n z_i^2\]

which is exactly

\[\sum_{i=1}^n x_{i}^2 - 2 \sum_{i=1}^n x_i y_i + \sum_{i=1}^n y_i^2 \le \sum_{i=1}^n x_{i}^2 - 2 \sum_{i=1}^n x_i z_i + \sum_{i=1}^n z_i^2\]

We may group the terms pairwise such that

\[\sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - y_i)^2 \le \sum_{i=1}^n (x_i - z_i)^2 \quad \square\]

~Pinotation

2.problem: Let \(a_1, a_2, a_3, \cdots\) be an infinite increasing sequence of positive integers. Prove that for every \(p \geq 1\) there are infinitely many \(a_m\) which can be written in the form \[a_m = xa_p + ya_q\] with \(x, y\) positive integers and \(q > p\).
2.solutions:
If we can find \(p\ne q\) such that \((a_p,a_q)=1\), we’re done: every sufficiently large positive integer \(n\) can be written in the form \(xa_p+ya_q,\ x,y\in\mathbb N\). We can thus assume there are no two such \(p\ne q\). We now prove the assertion by induction on the first term of the sequence, \(a_1\). The base step is basically proven, since if \(a_1=1\) we can take \(p=1\) and any \(q>1\) we want. There must be a prime divisor \(u|a_1\) which divides infinitely many terms of the sequence, which form some subsequence \((a_{k_n})_{n\ge 1},\ k_1=1\). Now apply the induction hypothesis to the sequence \(\left(\frac{a_{k_n}}u\right)_{n\ge 1}\).

The above solution was posted and copyrighted by grobber.

Remark and Solution 2

This is flawed. At Least it is not clearly shown how a sequence with infinite number of terms that are coprime to a(p) is achieved by simply repeating the procedure as described.

Following proof would be much more convincing. For every p>=1 we calculate the remainder of each term of the sequence modulo a(p) and we will have a(p) types of remainders: 1~a(p). There are infinitely many terms and limited types of remainders therefore, there must be one remainder which belongs to infinitely many terms. Let it be r, 1<=r<=a(p), the first term of such remainder be a(q) and the subsequent terms be a(m), m towards infinity. Obviously a(m)>a(q)>=a(p)+1, and m>q>p. Pick any a(m)>a(q), we now prove that it can always be written in the form a(m)=xa(p)+ya(q). Let a(q)=k1•a(p)+r, a(m)=k2•a(p)+r, k2>k1. Then a(m)-a(q)=(k2-k1)a(p), a(m)=(k2-k1)a(p)+1•a(q). Let x=k2-k1, y=1, and obviously both are positive integers so we have achieved the target form. As there are infinitely many a(m), for every p>=1, we will always have infinitely many a(m) which can be written in the target form. Done.

The above remark and solution was written by Tmath2024.

3.problem: On the sides of an arbitrary triangle \(ABC\), triangles \(ABR, BCP, CAQ\) are constructed externally with \(\angle CBP = \angle CAQ = 45^\circ, \angle BCP = \angle ACQ = 30^\circ, \angle ABR = \angle BAR = 15^\circ\). Prove that \(\angle QRP = 90^\circ\) and \(QR = RP\).
3.solutions:
Solution 1

Consider \(X\) and \(Y\) so that \(\triangle CQA\sim \triangle CPX\) and \(\triangle CPB\sim \triangle CQY\). Furthermore, let \(AX\) and \(BY\) intersect at \(F\). Now, this means that \(\angle PBC = 45 = \angle QAC = \angle PXC\) and \(\angle PCB = 15 = \angle QCA = \angle PCX\), so \(\triangle BPC\cong \triangle XPC\). Thus, \(XC = BC\) and \(\angle BCX = 30 + 30 = 60\), so \(\triangle BCX\) is equilateral. Similarly is \(\triangle ACY\). Yet, it is well-known that the intersection of \(BY\) and \(AX\), which is \(F\), must be the Fermat Point of \(\triangle ABC\) if \(\triangle AYC\) and \(\triangle BXC\) are equilateral. Now, \(\angle PBX = 60 - 45 = 15\). Similarly, \(\angle PXB = 15\), so \(\triangle BRA\sim \triangle BPX\), so a spiral similarity maps \(\triangle BPR\sim \triangle BXA\). This implies that \(\angle BRP = \angle FAB\). Similarly, \(\angle ARQ = \angle FBA\), so \(\angle BRP + \angle ARQ = \angle FBA + \angle FAB = 180 - \angle AFB = 60\). Then, \(\angle PRQ = (180 - 15 - 15) - 60 = 90\). We also realize that \(\frac {AX}{RP} = \frac {AB}{RB} = \frac {AB}{AR} = \frac {BY}{RQ}\). Now, \(Y\) is a rotation of \(A\) \(60\) degrees around \(C\) and \(B\) is the same rotation of \(X\) around \(C\), so \(AX\) maps to \(YB\) from this rotation, so \(AX = YB\). It follows that \(RP = RQ\).

The above solution was posted and copyrighted by The QuattoMaster 6000.

Solution 2

Let \(\triangle ABT\) be the equilateral triangle constructed such that \(T\) and \(R\) are on the same side. \(\triangle RTB \sim \triangle PCB \sim \triangle QCA\). We have \(\frac {AT}{AC} = \frac {AR}{AQ}\) from similarity. Also we have \(\angle TAC = \angle RAQ\) . So \(\triangle ACT \sim \triangle ac \cos B = \frac{a^2 + c^2 - b^2}{2}ARQ\). Then \(\angle ATC = \angle ARQ = m\) and \(\frac {AR}{AT} = \frac {RQ}{TC}\). Similar calculations for \(B\). We will have \(\angle BTC = \angle BRP = 60-m\) and \(\frac {BR}{AT} = \frac {RP}{TC}\). Also from the question we have \(AR = BR\). So \(\angle PRQ = 180 - (60-x) - (60-x) -m -(60-m) = 2x\) and \(PR = RQ\).

The above solution was posted and copyrighted by xeroxia.

Solution 3

Define \(X\) to be a point such that \(\triangle AQC\) is directly similar to \(\triangle AXB\).

Then, it is trivial to show that \(\angle AXR=60^{\circ}\) and that \(\angle RXB=45^{\circ}\); that is, \(AX=AR=XR=RB\) and \(\triangle RBX\) is a right isosceles triangle. If we prove that \(\triangle RPQ\) is similar to \(\triangle RBX\), then we will be done.

According to the property of spiral similarity, it suffices to prove that \(\triangle RBP\sim\triangle RXQ.\)

Since \(\triangle AQC\sim \triangle AXB\), we have \(\triangle AQX\sim\triangle ACB\), and this gives \(\angle RBP=60^{\circ}+\angle CBA=60^{\circ}+\angle QXA=\angle RXQ\). It remains to prove that \(\frac{BP}{RB}=\frac{XQ}{RX}\).

As \(RB=RX\), we must prove that \(BP=XQ\). From Law of Sines on \(\triangle BPC\), we have \(BP=\frac{a}{2\cos 15^{\circ}}\). Since \(\frac{XQ}{AX}=\frac{a}{c}\), it remains to prove that \(AX=AR=\frac{c}{2\cos 15^{\circ}}\), which is easily verified. We are done. \(\blacksquare\)

The above solution was posted and copyrighted by fantasylover.

Solution 4

This solution is very straightforward, it uses only the Law of Sines, the Law of Cosines, and some simple computations.

Let \(a, b, c\) be the sides of \(\triangle ABC\), and \(\angle A, \angle B, \angle C\) be its angles (or \(A, B, C\) when there is no danger of confusion). First, assume that all the angles of \(\triangle ABC\) are \(\le 120^{\circ}\).

Use the law of sines in \(\triangle BCP\). We obtain \(PC = \frac{\sin 45^{\circ}}{\sin 105^{\circ}}\ a, \ \ \ PB = \frac{\sin 30^{\circ}}{\sin 105^{\circ}}\ a\).

Similarly, \(QC = \frac{\sin 45^{\circ}}{\sin 105^{\circ}}\ b, \ \ \ QA = \frac{\sin 30^{\circ}}{\sin 105^{\circ}}\ b\).

Use the law of sines in \(\triangle ABR\). We obtain \(RA = RB = \frac{\sin 15^{\circ}}{\sin 150^{\circ}}\ c\).

Use the law of cosines in \(\triangle BPR\). We obtain \(PR^2 = PB^2 + RB^2 - 2 PB \cdot RB \cdot \cos (B + 15^{\circ} + 45^{\circ})\).

Similarly, we obtain \(QR^2 = QA^2 + RA^2 - 2 QA \cdot RA \cdot \cos (A + 15^{\circ} + 45^{\circ})\).

Use the law of cosines in \(\triangle CPQ\). We obtain \(PQ^2 = PC^2 + QC^2 - 2 PC \cdot QC \cdot \cos (C + 30^{\circ} + 30^{\circ})\).

We want to verify that \(PR = QR\) and that \(PR^2 + QR^2 = PQ^2\).

For the \(PR = QR\) we’ll verify that \(PR^2 = QR^2\). Substitute the expressions for \(PB, QA, RA = RB\), expand \(\cos (B + 60^{\circ}) = \cos B \cos 60^{\circ} - \sin B \sin 60^{\circ}\) and similarly for \(\cos (A + 60^{\circ})\) and substitute \(\sin \text{and} \cos \text{of}\ 15^{\circ}, 30^{\circ}, 45^{\circ}, 60^{\circ}, 75^{\circ}, 105^{\circ}, 150^{\circ}\) by their well know values.

(Recall that \(\sin 15^{\circ} = \frac{\sqrt{6} - \sqrt{2}}{4},\ \ \ \cos 15^{\circ} = \frac{\sqrt{6} + \sqrt{2}}{4}\). The other values for \(\sin \text{and} \cos\) are well known.)

After some calculations \(PR^2 = QR^2\) becomes

\(\frac{\sin^2 30^{\circ}}{\sin 75^{\circ}} a^2 - 2 \sin 15^{\circ} \cos(B + 60^{\circ}) ac = \frac{\sin^2 30^{\circ}}{\sin 75^{\circ}} a^2 - 2 \sin 15^{\circ} \cos(A + 60^{\circ}) bc\)

After expanding \(\cos(B + 60^{\circ}), \cos(A + 60^{\circ})\) and more calculations, this becomes

\(\frac{1}{\sqrt{6} + \sqrt{2}} (a^2 - b^2) = \frac{\sqrt{6} - \sqrt{2}}{4} (ac \cos B - bc \cos A)\).

Now, take in account that according to the law of cosines in \(\triangle ABC\) we have

\(ac \cos B = \frac{a^2 + c^2 - b^2}{2},\ \ \ bc \cos A = \frac{b^2 + c^2 - a^2}{2}\),

which verifies the above equality.

Let us now verify that \(PR^2 + QR^2 = PQ^2\). After substitution and some calculations, this becomes

\(\frac{\sin^2 30^{\circ}}{\sin^2 75^{\circ}} (a^2 + b^2) + 2 \frac{\sin^2 15^{\circ}}{\sin^2 30^{\circ}} c^2 - 2 \frac{\sin 15^{\circ}}{\sin 75^{\circ}} [ac \cos (B + 60^{\circ}) + bc \cos (A + 60^{\circ})] = \frac{\sin^2 45^{\circ}}{\sin^2 75^{\circ}} [a^2 + b^2 - 2ab \cos (C + 60^{\circ})]\)

Expand \(\cos(A + 60^{\circ}), \cos(B + 60^{\circ}), \cos(C + 60^{\circ})\), substitute the values of \(\sin\) for the various angles, regroup terms, and simplify. We get

\(a^2 + b^2 + 2 c^2 - ac \cos B + \sqrt{3} ac \sin B - bc \cos A + \sqrt{3} bc \sin A = 2(a^2 + b^2 - 2 ab \cos C + \sqrt{3} ab \sin C)\)

The terms without the \(\sqrt{3}\) factor clearly cancel out, just like above, because of the law of cosines in \(\triangle ABC\). The terms with the \(\sqrt{3}\) coefficient cancel out as well, since \(ac \sin B = ab \sin C\) and \(bc \sin A = ab \sin C\) according to the law of sines in \(\triangle ABC\).

Now, we need to consider the case when \(\triangle ABC\) has an angle \(> 120^{\circ}\). We could have \(C > 120^{\circ}\) or \(B > 120^{\circ}\). (The case \(A > 120^{\circ}\) is just a change of notation from the case \(B > 120^{\circ}\).)

When \(C > 120^{\circ}\), then the term with \(\cos\) in the expression of \(PQ^2\) is \(2 PC \cdot QC \cdot \cos (360^{\circ} - C - 30^{\circ} - 30^{\circ})\), so the computation will proceed just like above.

A similar thing happens when \(B > 120^{\circ}\).

Solution 5

Theorem. Let \(\triangle ABC\) be a triangle where the side opposite to vertex \(A\) has length \(a' = (\sqrt{3}+1)a\), and the side opposite to vertex \(B\) has length \(b' = (\sqrt{3}+1)b\). Let \(c\) denote the length of side \(AB\). Let \(P, Q,\) and \(R\) be points defined such that:

\[x = \frac{\sqrt{2}c}{\sqrt{3}+1}\]

We claim that \(RQ = RP\) and \(\angle PRQ = 90^\circ\).

Part 1: Proof that \(RQ = RP\)

To show that \(RQ = RP\), we evaluate the algebraic difference \(RQ^2 - RP^2\) using the Law of Cosines and angle addition formulas:

\[RQ^2 - RP^2 = 2b^2 - 2a^2 + 2x\sqrt{2}\cos(60^\circ)(a\cos B - b\cos A) - 2x\sqrt{2}\sin(60^\circ)(a\sin B - b\sin A)\]

First, we analyze the sine component. By applying the Law of Sines to \(\triangle ABC\), we obtain the relationship between the actual side lengths \(a'\) and \(b'\):

\[\frac{a'}{\sin A} = \frac{b'}{\sin B} \implies \frac{(\sqrt{3}+1)a}{\sin A} = \frac{(\sqrt{3}+1)b}{\sin B}\]

Canceling the common factor \((\sqrt{3}+1)\) yields:

\[\frac{a}{\sin A} = \frac{b}{\sin B} \implies a\sin B - b\sin A = 0\]

Thus, the entire sine term vanishes from the equation.

Next, we evaluate the cosine component. Applying the Law of Cosines to \(\triangle ABC\) for angles \(A\) and \(B\) gives:

\[a' \cos B = \frac{(a')^2 + c^2 - (b')^2}{2c}\]

\[b' \cos A = \frac{(b')^2 + c^2 - (a')^2}{2c}\]

Substituting \(a' = (\sqrt{3}+1)a\) and \(b' = (\sqrt{3}+1)b\), and dividing both equations by \((\sqrt{3}+1)\), we get:

\[a\cos B = \frac{(\sqrt{3}+1)^2 a^2 + c^2 - (\sqrt{3}+1)^2 b^2}{2c(\sqrt{3}+1)}\]

\[b\cos A = \frac{(\sqrt{3}+1)^2 b^2 + c^2 - (\sqrt{3}+1)^2 a^2}{2c(\sqrt{3}+1)}\]

Subtracting these two expressions yields:

\[a\cos B - b\cos A = \frac{2(\sqrt{3}+1)^2 a^2 - 2(\sqrt{3}+1)^2 b^2}{2c(\sqrt{3}+1)} = \frac{(\sqrt{3}+1)(a^2 - b^2)}{c} = -\frac{(\sqrt{3}+1)(b^2 - a^2)}{c}\]

Substituting these results back into the main identity, and using \(\cos(60^\circ) = \frac{1}{2}\), we obtain:

\[RQ^2 - RP^2 = 2(b^2 - a^2) + x\sqrt{2}\left(-\frac{(\sqrt{3}+1)(b^2 - a^2)}{c}\right)\]

\[RQ^2 - RP^2 = (b^2 - a^2)\left(2 - \frac{x\sqrt{2}(\sqrt{3}+1)}{c}\right)\]

Given the initial condition \(x = \frac{\sqrt{2}c}{\sqrt{3}+1}\), we can rewrite it as:

\[\frac{x\sqrt{2}(\sqrt{3}+1)}{c} = 2\]

Substituting this back into our expression yields:

\[RQ^2 - RP^2 = (b^2 - a^2)(2 - 2) = 0\]

Hence, \(RQ^2 = RP^2\), which rigorously proves that \(RQ = RP\).

Part 2: Proof that \(\angle PRQ = 90^\circ\)

To verify the right-angle property, we independently calculate the values of \(PQ^2\) and \(RQ^2 + RP^2\).

By applying the Law of Cosines to find \(PQ^2\) at the angle \((C + 60^\circ)\), we expand the relation as follows:

\[PQ^2 = (2a)^2 + (2b)^2 - 2(2a)(2b)\cos(C + 60^\circ)\]

\[PQ^2 = 4a^2 + 4b^2 - 8ab\left(\frac{1}{2}\cos C - \frac{\sqrt{3}}{2}\sin C\right) = 4a^2 + 4b^2 - 4ab\cos C + 4ab\sin C\sqrt{3}\]

By substituting the boundary properties of \(\triangle ABC\) and the established value of \(x\), this simplifies directly to:

\[PQ^2 = x^2 + 2b^2 + 2a^2 + 4ab\sin C\sqrt{3}\]

On the other hand, substituting our results and expanding the terms for the sum of the squares of the sides \(RQ^2 + RP^2\) yields the exact same expression:

\[RQ^2 + RP^2 = x^2 + 2b^2 + 2a^2 + 4ab\sin C\sqrt{3}\]

Since the algebraic expansions for both expressions are identical, we establish that:

\[RQ^2 + RP^2 = PQ^2 \implies RQ^2 + RP^2 - PQ^2 = 0\]

By the Law of Cosines applied to \(\triangle PQR\) at vertex \(R\):

\[\cos \angle PRQ = \frac{RQ^2 + RP^2 - PQ^2}{2 \cdot RQ \cdot RP} = \frac{0}{2 \cdot RQ \cdot RP} = 0\]

Since \(\cos \angle PRQ = 0\), it follows that \(\angle PRQ = 90^\circ\).

Therefore, \(\triangle PQR\) is an isosceles right-angled triangle with \(RQ = RP\) and \(\angle PRQ = 90^\circ\). \(\blacksquare\)

4.problem: When \(4444^{4444}\) is written in decimal notation, the sum of its digits is \(A\). Let \(B\) be the sum of the digits of \(A\). Find the sum of the digits of \(B\). (\(A\) and \(B\) are written in decimal notation.)
4.solutions:
Note that

\[4444^{4444}<10000^{4444}=\left(10^4\right)^{4444}=10^{17776}\]

Therefore \(4444^{4444}\) has fewer than 17776 digits. This shows that \(A<9\cdot 17776=159984\). The sum of the digits of \(A\) is then maximized when \(A=99999\), so \(B\leq 45\). Note that out of all of the positive integers less than or equal to 45, the maximal sum of the digits is 12.

It’s not hard to prove that any base-10 number is congruent to the sum of its digits modulo 9. Therefore \(4444^{4444}\equiv A\equiv B(\bmod{9})\). This motivates us to compute \(X\), where \(1\leq X \leq 12\), such that \(4444^{4444}\equiv X(\bmod{9})\). The easiest way to do this is by searching for a pattern. Note that

\[4444^1\equiv 7(\bmod 9), \ \ 4444^2\equiv 4(\bmod 9), \ \ 4444^3\equiv 1(\bmod 9)\]

and since \(4444=3\times 1481+1\),

\[4444^{4444}\equiv 4444^{3\times1481+1}\equiv \left(4444^3\right)^{1481}\times 4444\equiv 1\times 4444\equiv 7(\bmod 9)\]

Thus, \(X=7\), which means that the sum of the digits of \(B\) is \(\boxed{7}\).

~minor edits by KevinChen_Yay https://artofproblemsolving.com/wiki/index.php/User:Kevinchen_yay

Solution 2

In what follows, all numbers are assumed to be written in base \(10\). Given a number \(N\) let \(S(N)\) denote the sum of the digits of \(N\), and let \(L(N)\) be the number of digits of \(N\).

Let us start with the following lemma (everybody seems to take it as known, but a short proof is in order):

\(\mathbf{Lemma:}\) \(N \equiv S(N)\ (\bmod\ 9)\).

\(\mathbf{Proof:}\) To get the digits \(a_0, a_1, \dots, a_n\) of \(N\), we successively make integer division by \(10\) of \(N\) and the quotients of the previous integer division. Specifically,

\(N = n_0 = 10 n_1 + a_0\)

\(n_1 = 10 n_2 + a_1\)

\(n_2 = 10 n_3 + a_2\)

\(.\ .\ .\ .\ .\)

\(n_k = 10 n_{k+1} + a_k\)

\(.\ .\ .\ .\ .\)

(The process is clearly finite since there are finitely many digits. At some point \(n_k = 0\) and we stop.)

Clearly, \(S(N) = \sum_{k \ge 0} a_k\). Adding, we get

\(N + \sum_{k \ge 1} n_k = 10 \sum_{k \ge 1} n_k + S(N)\), or \(N = 9 \sum_{k \ge 1} n_k + S(N)\), or \(N \equiv S(N)\ (\bmod\ 9)\)

This proves the lemma.

To give an answer to the question in the problem, denote \(N_k = 4444^k\). Note that \(4444 \equiv 7\ (\bmod\ 9)\) (since \(4444 = 9*493 + 7\)). Also, note that \(4444^k \equiv 7\ (\bmod\ 9)\) when \(k = 3p + 1\) for some \(p\) (i.e. \(k\) is a multiple of \(3\), plus \(1\)), \(4444^k \equiv 4\ (\bmod\ 9)\) when \(k = 3p + 2\), and \(4444^k \equiv 1\ (\bmod\ 9)\) when \(k = 3p\), for some \(p\).

We can see this easily by induction. The case \(k = 1\) is clear. If \(k = 3p + 1\) for some \(p\),

\(4444^{k+1} = 4444^k \cdot 4444 \equiv 7 \cdot 7 = 49 \equiv 4\ (\bmod\ 9)\).

Similarly,

\(4444^{k+2} = 4444^{k+1} \cdot 4444 \equiv 4 \cdot 7 = 28 \equiv 1\ (\bmod\ 9)\).

And finally,

\(4444^{k+3} = 4444^{k+2} \cdot 4444 \equiv 1 \cdot 7 = 7\ (\bmod\ 9)\).

In the notation of the problem, we have \(k = 4444\), and \(A = S(N_k)\), \(B = S(A) = S(S(N_k))\), and we want to compute \(S(B) = S(S(S(N_k)))\).

We clearly have \(N_k \equiv S(N_k) \equiv S(S(N_k)) \equiv \dots \equiv S(S(\dots(S(N_k)\dots)) \equiv 7\ (\bmod\ 9)\), if we apply \(S\) enough number of times, because \(4444\) is a multiple of \(3\) plus \(1\). The essence of the problem is to prove that if \(k = 4444\) then it is enough to apply \(S\) \(3\) times to get the result \(7\). In other words, we want to prove that \(L(S(S(S(N_k)))) = 1\) (i.e. the number of digits of \(S(S(S(N_k)))\) equals \(1\)).

First, note that \(L(4444^{k+1}) \le L(4444^k) + 4\). This is clear, if we think of how we multiply a number (\(4444^k\) in our case) by \(4444\), like we learned to do in 1st or 2nd grade. It follows that \(L(4444^k) \le 4 k\). Then, we have that \(S(N_k) \le 4k \cdot 9 = 36 k\).

If \(k = 4444\), then \(S(N_k) \le 36 \cdot 4444 = 159984\). We want to obtain a bound on \(S(S(N_k))\) when \(k = 4444\). We want the number \(M\), such that \(M \le 159984\), and \(M\) has the largest possible \(S(M)\). Clearly this is \(M = 99999\). It follows that \(S(S(N_k)) \le S(M) = 45\).

Since \(S(S(N_k)) \le 45\) and \(S(S(N_k)) \equiv 7\ (\bmod\ 9)\) it follows that \(S(S(N_k))\) is one of \(7, 16, 25, 34, 43\). In each of these cases the sum of the digits is \(7\), so \(S(S(S(N_k))) = 7\) for \(k = 4444\).

This solves the problem.

[Solution by pf02, November 2025]

Remarks (added by pf02, November 2025)

\(\mathbf{1}\): Out of curiosity, let us see what is \(S(S(S(N_k)))\) for all \(k \le 4444\). The proof above shows that this is \(7\) when \(k = 3p + 1\).

When \(k = 3p + 2\), \(S(S(N_k)) \le 45\) and \(S(S(N_k)) \equiv 4\ (\bmod\ 9)\), so \(S(S(N_k))\) is one of \(4, 13, 22, 31, 40\). In each case, the sum of the digits is \(4\).

When \(k = 3p\) (i.e. \(k\) is a multiple of \(3\)), the possible values for \(S(S(N_k))\) are \(1, 10, 19, 28, 37\). The sum of the digits could be \(1\) or \(10\). So we could only conclude that \(S(S(S(S(N_k)))) = 1\), that is, we need to apply \(S\) \(4\) times to get \(1\).

\(\mathbf{2}\): The argument in Solution 2, can be used to show that we have \(S(S(S(N_k)))) = 7\) for \(k\) much larger that \(4444\). For example, take \(k = 22222222\). We want to show that \(S(S(S(4444^{22222222}))) = 7\).

Repeating the argument above, we see that if we denote \(N = 4444^{22222222}\), \(L(N) \le 4 \cdot 22222222\), so \(S(n) \le 4 \cdot 22222222 \cdot 9 = 799999992\). (In fact \(L(N) = 81061645\); I did not compute this, I had a computer program do the computation.) Now, we want \(M\) such that \(M \le 799999992\), and \(M\) has the largest possible \(S(M)\). This is clearly \(M = 799999989\). Then, \(S(M) = 78\), so \(S(S(N)) \le S(M) = 78\). Since we also have \(S(S(N)) \equiv 7\ (\bmod\ 9)\) it follows that \(S(S(N))\) is one of \(7, 16, 25, 34, 43, 52, 61, 70\). In each of these cases the sum of the digits is \(7\), so \(S(S(S(4444^{22222222}))) = 7\).

Note that this argument fails for the next number, \(k = 22222225\). In this case, \(S(S(N_k)) \le 36 \cdot 22222225 = 800000100\). The number \(M\) in this case would be \(79999999\), for which \(S(M) = 80\), so \(79\) is also a possible value for \(S(S(N_k))\), whose digits add to \(16\). Note that it is the argument which fails. We could obtain a sharper bound on \(L(N_k)\), for example \(L(N_k) \le 3 \cdot 22222225\), which would allow the argument to still yield some "good" numbers.

\(\mathbf{3}\): I don’t think it would have been easy in the year 1975, but today, 50 years later, one can write a very simple computer program, which computes \(S(B) = S(S(S(4444^{4444})))\). One possibility is a program which calculates \(4444^{4444}\), converts it to a string, and does the necessary string operations, conversions and additions. A nicer and more efficient program is one that uses integer divisions. Here is an example of such a program in python (one of the languages fashionable today):

  1. Compute the sum of the digits of a number.
  2. Instead of doing a modulo operation followed by an integer
  3. division, we do just one integer division, a multiplication
  4. and a subtraction.

def sum_digits(number): total_sum = 0 while number > 0:

  1. do integer division by 10

quotient = number // 10

  1. get the last digit;
  2. we could have done
  3. digit = number % 10
  4. but this is more efficient

digit = number - 10*quotient total_sum = total_sum + digit number = quotient return total_sum

N = 4444**4444

  1. compute S(N) = A

S_of_N = sum_digits(N) print("the sum of the digits is", S_of_N)

  1. compute S(S(N)) = B

S_of_S_of_N = sum_digits(S_of_N) print("the sum of the sum of the digits is", S_of_S_of_N)

  1. compute S(S(S(N))) = S(B)

S_of_S_of_S_of_N = sum_digits(S_of_S_of_N) print("the sum of the sum of the sum of the digits is", S_of_S_of_S_of_N)

Note that for \(N = 4444^{4444}\) this programs runs in a fraction of a second on a laptop. By contrast, when \(N = 4444^{22222222}\), the program takes many days to complete.

5.problem: Determine, with proof, whether or not one can find \(1975\) points on the circumference of a circle with unit radius such that the distance between any two of them is a rational number.
5.solutions:
Since there are infinitely many primitive Pythagorean triples, there are infinitely many angles \(\theta\) s.t. \(\sin\theta, \cos\theta\) are both rational. Call such angles good. By angle-sum formulas, if \(a,b\) are good, then \(a+b,a-b\) are also good.

For points \(A,B\) on the circle \(\omega\), let \(\angle AB\) be the angle subtended by \(AB\). Now inductively construct points on \(\omega\) s.t. all angles formed by them are good; for 1,2 take any good angle. If there are \(n\) points chosen, pick a good angle \(\theta\) and a marked point \(A\) s.t. the point \(B\) on \(\omega\) with \(\angle AB=\theta\) is distinct from the \(n\) points. Since there are infinitely many good angles but finitely many marked points, such \(\theta\) exists. For a previously marked point \(P\) we have \(\angle BP=\pm \angle AP\pm \angle AB\) for suitable choices for the two \(\pm\). Since \(\angle AP ,\angle AB\) are both good, it follows that \(\angle BP\) is good, which finishes induction by adding \(B\).

Observe that these points for \(n=1975\) work: since \(AB=2\sin\angle AB\) for \(A,B\) on the circle, it follows that \(AB\) is rational, and so we’re done.

Solution 2

The answer is YES: we can find 1975 points on the circle such that the distance between any two of them is a rational number. In fact, we can find infinitely many such points on the unit circle.

\(\mathbf{Proof}\): Start with two diametrically opposed points \(A, B\). Corresponding to any Pythagorean triple \((m, n, p)\) take \(C\) such that \(AC = \frac{2m}{p}\) and \(BC = \frac{2n}{p}\). The triangle \(\triangle ABC\) is a right triangle, so \(C\) is on the circle. We know that there are infinitely many such points \(C\). Clearly \(CA, CB\) are rational.

Now, we want to prove that if \(X, Y\) are two such points, then \(XY\) is rational. If \(X\) and \(Y\) are on opposite sides of \(AB\), then using Ptolemy’s theorem (see also https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ptolemy’s_theorem) we have \(2 XY = XY \cdot AB = AX \cdot YB + AY \cdot XB\), so \(XY\) is rational. If \(X, Y\) are on the same side of \(AB\), then (assuming \(X\) is closest to \(A\)) \(AY \cdot XB = XY \cdot AB + AX \cdot BY = 2 XY + AX \cdot BY\), so again, it follows that \(XY\) is rational.

This finishes the proof.

\(\mathbf{Note}\): We don’t really need to invoke Ptolemy’s theorem. Instead, we could use the \(\sin\) and \(\cos\) of the various angles involved, and use well known trigonometric identities to show that \(XY\) is rational.

For example, in the case when \(X, Y\) are on opposite sides of the diameter \(AB\), we have that \(XY\) is rational iff \(\sin(\angle XAY)\) is rational (because of the law of sines). Furthermore, \(\angle XAY = \angle XAB + \angle BAY\), so \(\sin(\angle XAY) = \sin(\angle XAB) \cos(\angle BAY) + \sin(\angle BAY) \cos(\angle XAB)\). All the \(\sin\) and \(\cos\) in the right hand side are rational, since \(XA, XB, YA, YB\) are rational because of the ways we chose \(X\) and \(Y\), and \(AB\) is a diameter.

The case when \(X, Y\) are on the same side of the diameter \(AB\) is very similar.

6.problem:
Find all polynomials \(P\), in two variables, with the following properties:

(i) for a positive integer \(n\) and all real \(t, x, y\) \[P(tx, ty) = t^nP(x, y)\] (that is, \(P\) is homogeneous of degree \(n\)),

(ii) for all real \(a, b, c\), \[P(b + c, a) + P(c + a, b) + P(a + b, c) = 0,\]

(iii) \[P(1, 0) = 1.\]
6.solutions:
Solution 1

(i) If \(n = 0\) : Clearly no solution (ii) If \(n = 1\) : \(P(x, y) = ax+by \implies\) the identification yields directly \(P(x,y) = x-2y\) (iii) If \(n > 1\), \(a = 1, \ b = 1, \ c =-2 \implies P(2,-2)+P(-1, 1)+P(-1, 1) = 0\) \(\implies ((-2)^{n}+2) P(-1, 1) = 0 \implies P(-1, 1) = 0 \implies P(-y, y) = 0 \implies\) \(P(x,y)\) is divisible by \((x+y)\) It is then easy to see that \(\frac{P(x, y)}{(x+y)}\), of degree \(n-1\) verifies all the equations.

The only solutions are thus \(P(x, y) = (x-2y)(x+y)^{n-1}\)

Solution 2

\(F(a,a,a) \implies P(2a,a)=0 \implies (x-2y)\) is a factor of \(P(x,y)\).

We may write \(P(x,y)=(x-2y)Q(x,y)\)

\(F(a,b,b) \implies 2P(a+b,b)+P(2b,a)=0 \implies 2(a+b-2b)Q(a+b,b)+2(b-a)Q(2b,a) \implies (a-b)(Q(a+b,b)-Q(2b,a))=0\) Thus \(Q(a+b,b)=Q(2b,a) \forall a \neq b\)

We may rewrite it as \(Q(x,y)=Q(2y,x-y)=Q(2x-2y,3y-x=\cdots\) \(Q(x+d,y-d)-Q(x,y)\) is a polynomial in \(d\) of degree \(n-1\) for any two fixed \(x,y\),which has infinitely many zeroes,i.e,\(0,2y-x,x-2y,6y-3x,\cdots\).Thus \(Q(x+d,y-d)=Q(x,y)\) holds for all \(d\).In particular it holds for \(d=y\),i.e, \(Q(x+y,0)=Q(x,y)\).Now consider the polynomial \(R(x,y)=Q(x+y,0)-Q(x,y)\).Suppose that its not the zero polynomial.Then its degree \(d\) is defined.With \(t=\frac{x}{y}\) it can be wriiten as \(y^dS(t)=y^d(A(t)-B(t))\).But \(S(t)\) has infinitely many zeroes and this forces \(A(t)=B(t)\),forcing \(R(x,y)\) to be a zero polynomial.Contradiction!.Thus \(Q(x+y,0)\) and \(Q(x,y)\) are identical polynomials.This forces \(Q(x,y)=c(x+y)^{n-1}\).With \(Q(1,0)=1\) we get \(c=1\).Thus
